intro: Ames is a university town in central Iowa, home to Iowa State University, on the creeks and wooded bottoms that run down to the Skunk River. A reader sent us one of its trees: a lone American sycamore on a grassy bank by the road, whose upper limbs have shed their brown bark and stand bone-white against the dark woods behind it in winter.

trees.name: The White Sycamore of Ames

location.address: Grassy bank beside the road, Ames, Iowa

trees.story:
In winter, when every other tree on the bank behind it is a grey smudge, this one looks as if it had been painted white. A reader in Ames, Iowa, sent us the photograph from the sidewalk across the road, and it is easy to see why they stopped.

It is an American sycamore, the great tree of Midwestern creek bottoms, and the colour is its own doing. As a sycamore grows, its brown outer bark flakes away from the upper trunk and limbs in patches, leaving the pale inner bark bare, so an old tree turns whiter the higher you look. Here the lower trunk is still mottled brown and cream, and above it the limbs reach out sideways in long, crooked arms, bone-white against the dark woods, the lowest almost sweeping the grass.

This one has the bank to itself, which is why its crown has spread so wide and even. We do not know its age, girth or who planted it, if anyone did; sycamores often seed themselves along streams. If you know the tree, tell us here and we will put your words on the page.

Come in winter, on a grey day, when the white is brightest.
